Beijing's Foreign Ministry said this week it was in contact with Washington and Moscow about the possibility.

The Busan agreement, which reflected calming tensions between the superpowers after they had exchanged tariff escalations earlier in 2025, required China to purchase U.S. soybeans this year and through 2028.
China also agreed to suspend new export controls on rare earths and to issue general licences for exports of the materials.
The accord initially covered one year, but the two sides extended the ceasefire through to January 10, 2027, during Mr. Jinping’s September visit to the White House.

articles.title: United States offers $20 million reward for information on 'Iran's nuclear program': CENTCOM
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: U.S. State Department program, Rewards for Justice, gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward

Washington is offering a $20 million reward "and possible relocation" for information about Iran's nuclear program, the U.S. Military said Friday (November 6, 2026), as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war.

A U.S. State Department program, Rewards for Justice, "is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community," U.S. Central Command said on X .
The program was established in 1984 under the State Department's national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests.

In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran's "lack of compliance with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges.
It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly said U.S. forces have effectively obliterated Iran's nuclear program.

"If we didn't hit Iran, you wouldn't have Israel today," Mr. Trump said Friday (November 6, 2026) night in West Palm Beach, Florida. "If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East."
But the President also said Iran, which he stressed has had its economy and Military severely damaged over eight months of war, is eager to end the conflict.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting.
And on Tuesday (November 6, 2026) Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his Government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.

Earlier this week Mr. Trump said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.

articles.title: Secret Service arrests man near White House after he said he heard voices telling him to kill Trump
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: U.S. officials say the suspect, Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, then went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican President

The U.S. Secret Service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill President Donald Trump .
The arrest Thursday night (November 7, 2026) happened after Secret Service officers approached a man "acting suspicious" in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement.
U.S. officials say the suspect, Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, then went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation's capital and kill the Republican President.
Shortly after, officers discovered the suspect's vehicle had been reported stolen and he had three different firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition.

This is the latest in a series of arrests the Secret Service and other law enforcement agencies have made against individuals who have threatened Trump or his family members' lives since he returned to office last year.

The statement described Chrinos as a migrant from Venezuela who is in the country illegally after entering the U.S. through Texas in March 2024. DHS said he has been charged and currently remains in U.S. Marshals Service custody.
The White House did not provide comment, instead referring to DHS and USSS.

"Thanks to our brave Secret Service officers, this illegal alien with three firearms in his vehicle was arrested near the White House before he could harm anyone," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the statement.

articles.title: Jay Rockefeller, heir to famed dynasty and healthcare advocate in U.S. Senate, dies at 89
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Jay Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John ‌D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of ​the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the ‌newspaper added.

Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his ​five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.

Mr. Rockefeller voted ⁠in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John ‌D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in ‌impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.

When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, ‌fight ⁠poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping ⁠the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.

Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.

In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully ​sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance ‌program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.

“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would ‌not seek a sixth Senate term.

Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating ​Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known ⁠then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.

New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in ‌impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.

When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, ‌fight ⁠poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping ⁠the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.

Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.

In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully ​sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance ‌program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.

“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would ‌not seek a sixth Senate term.

articles.title: U.S. military carries out fresh targeted strikes on Iran as Tehran weighs mediator's proposals
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: ‘They knocked out — they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device — and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five,’ says U.S. President Trump
President Donald Trump said the U.S. military on Friday (November 6, 2026) carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defence system.
Iran state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the crucial waterway for oil shipments.
Mr. Trump in an exchange with reporters described the military action as "minor".

"They knocked out — they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device — and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Mr. Trump told reporters shortly after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Friday (November 6) evening.

Mr. Trump did not offer further details about the target. U.S. officials have reported that most of Iran's air defence systems were destroyed or severely degraded during a June 2025 bombardment by Israel and in the early stages of the current conflict. U.S. officials have assessed that Iran would try to rebuild them and other military infrastructure over time.

The U.S. military also reported carrying out what it described as defensive strikes on Monday (November 2). Explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
Friday's (November 7) strikes are the first since Mr. Trump's Republican Party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday's (November 3) midterm elections in the U.S.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump's execution of the conflict and elevated fuel prices, a byproduct of the war that's affected nearly every sector of the global economy.
In the days since Republicans' shellacking at the polls, Mr. Trump has vacillated between threatening to "destroy" Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Earlier on Friday (November 6), officials from the two West Asian governments said Iran is reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the U.S. about Tehran's nuclear programme.

But one of the officials stressed that Iran, at least at the moment, remains unwilling to engage in negotiations with the Trump administration over its atomic activities until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.
The difference over Iran's nuclear programme is the thorniest issue and one that Mr. Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than eight-month-old war.

articles.title: The Siang dam and a threatened homeland
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Adi community has been protesting against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project in Arunachal Pradesh, saying it threatens their land, livelihoods, and civilisation. The agitation has turned violent in response to increasing use of force by the State authorities. The community alleges that the State government has used deceit, force, and threats to get consent for the feasibility study. Abhinay Lakshman reports on the resistance

A few kilometres from the entrance to Arunachal Pradesh’s Parong village, an unpaved road winds all the way down to the Siang river. At dusk, all that is visible at the beginning of the dirt road is the glint of freshly painted yellow barricades of the State police and the shine from the silver of the concertina wires that connect the barricades. The Central security forces who guard the check post here have two purposes — to respond to “unrest” and to stop anyone without “clearance” from proceeding to Siang’s waters.

Parong, in Siang district, is one of the three proposed sites identified by the State government for a Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) to begin work on the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), developed by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC).

articles.title: Keralam Child Development Centre gets ₹35-lakh grant to study autism-related parental grief
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Three-year project will examine chronic sorrow and coping mechanisms in ASD families.

The Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, has received an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-approved grant of ₹35 lakh for a three-year research project titled “Development and Validation of a Tool for Assessing Grief among Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.”
The project, led by CDC director Deepa Bhaskaran, aims to develop and validate a culturally relevant tool to assess grief among parents of children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD).

“The study will use focus group discussions and in-depth interviews involving parents of children with ASD, bereaved parents, professionals working with children with ASD, and members of the general population to understand the dimensions and cultural expressions of grief in the Indian context,” Dr. Bhaskaran said.

According to her, parents commonly experience shock, denial, fear, guilt, anger, sadness, and helplessness following their child’s diagnosis. The grief, described as chronic sorrow or non-finite grief, can recur at different stages of the child’s development, particularly when expected developmental milestones are not attained.

“The findings will help facilitate the identification of grief-related concerns among parents and support the development of appropriate grief counselling protocols and support group interventions, ultimately contributing to improved psychosocial well-being among families of children with ASD,” she said.
Inadequate social support compounds parental distress, she noted.

“There is a need for healthcare professionals to recognise and assess parents’ emotional well-being alongside the rehabilitation needs of children with autism. Early diagnosis, psychological support, and training for professionals to identify grief and help families develop coping strategies are vital,” she added.

articles.title: Supreme Court terms vehicular emissions major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.

Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.

On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.

On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.

articles.title: OpenAI to press ahead with data-centre expansion despite midterm sweep, CFO says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: One of the corporate faces of the AI boom, OpenAI has moved quickly ‌to counter fears that a shift in congressional power could slow the industry’s growth

OpenAI will press ahead with its US data-centre expansion plans despite a Democratic midterm sweep this week that has fuelled fears of tighter scrutiny ​of the facilities, its Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar told CNBC in an interview on Friday.

“When ‌I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how ​do we keep investing to meet customer demand,” Friar said. “We are ⁠going to keep building out those relationships with communities so we can get the compute we need,” she added.

One of the corporate faces of the AI boom, OpenAI has moved quickly ‌to counter fears that a shift in congressional power could slow the industry’s growth. It launched a charm offensive on Thursday to win ‌over communities as opposition to data centres becomes a rallying point for anxieties ‌about ⁠the technology.

As part of the efforts, OpenAI said, it will no ⁠longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites. It will also give residents access to construction plans and their potential effects.

Growing data-centre opposition was a crucial issue in the midterm ​elections. Democratic candidates, including Texas Governor-elect Gina ‌Hinojosa, made tighter scrutiny of the facilities a central campaign pledge. The Lone Star State is one of the fastest-growing data-center regions in the world.

Fears the Democratic sweep may slow construction of the facilities critical to the AI boom ‌wiped about $2.5 trillion off the US stock market on Thursday, as investors ​weighed the fallout for the chip, cloud and networking industries that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the spending frenzy.
Still, there are ⁠signs that tech giants remain committed to data-centre expansion plans despite the growing backlash.
Alphabet-owned Google said on Thursday it would invest $17 billion to build its first data centre ‌in Wyoming.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg News reported that ByteDance is considering expanding a data centre project in northeastern Brazil, a move that would strengthen its standing as Latin America’s leading builder of computing facilities.
Friar also told CNBC that OpenAI was raising fresh capital, pushing back against suggestions the ChatGPT maker had scaled back its fundraising ambitions amid the sharp AI stocks selloff.
The company is seeking fresh capital after ‌its business grew 70% quarter over quarter in the third quarter, with enterprise demand doubling over the ​same period, she said.
“It (the growth) is saying people are actually using AI and getting value from it,” Friar said.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh MPTC, ZPTC election results LIVE: TDP leads in multiple Zilla, Mandal Parishads
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha and other top officials are monitoring the counting.
A media person collapsed after suffering a heart attack while covering election updates at the Narsipatnam counting centre in Anakapalli district.
The journalist was identified as Chintakayala Giri, a representative for Andhra Jyothy from Nathavaram mandal.
The incident caused panic on the premises as medical emergency services were unavailable, highlighting a concerning lack of basic ambulance facilities at the key official venue.

Decision will be taken soon on conducting elections to 23 municipalities, State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha said. He said that elections to these Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) could not be held with the other 100 ULBs that went to polls on November 1, due to administrative and legal issues.

The counting of votes for the MPTC and ZPTC elections is proceeding smoothly in a peaceful atmosphere at the counting centers, with no untoward incidents reported so far, said District Collector Dr. S. Venkateswar.
He along with SP L. Subbarayudu addressed the media here on Saturday.

He said that the counting started by 8 a.m. and the results for 55 to 60 MPTCs across the district have been completed. The counting process for the remaining MPTCs is being expedited, and it is expected that the results for all MPTC seats in the district will be announced by 2 p.m. and those of ZPTC seats by 6 p.m.

Results of the MPTCs started to trickle in from Kurnool district and they went in favour of ruling TDP. TDP’s Lakshmanna has won as the MPTC of Erragudi in Krishnagiri mandal, Gummala Keerthi of TDP won as MPTC in M Kottala of Aluru mandal, and H Padma won as the MPTC of Dibbanakal in Adoni mandal.
TDP is leading in 14 out of 20 ZPTCs where counting of postal ballots was completed. There are 27 ZPTCs in Vizianagaram district. Counting is going on in another seven places.
Both TDP and YSRCP are hopeful of victory in Kotia group of villages of Salur mandal of Parvatipuram Manyam district where poll percentage is around 35%.
This, in spite of strong objection from Odisha over conduct of local body elections in those villages located at the AP-Odisha border.

The counting of votes for the Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituency (MPTC) and Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituency (ZPTC) elections began peacefully across Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR) district on Saturday, with the district administration making elaborate arrangements to ensure a smooth and transparent process.

articles.title: CPI(M) seeks anti-BJP alliance in Tripura civic polls to avoid vote split
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The CPI(M) has fielded 263 candidates across 345 wards, while the Congress has nominated candidates in 221 wards after seat-sharing talks between the two INDIA bloc partners failed

CPI(M) Tripura State Secretary Jitendra Chaudhury on Saturday (November 7, 2026) said the party was keen to forge an electoral understanding with democratic and secular parties to prevent a split in anti-BJP votes in the civic elections.
His statement came a day after the deadline for filing nominations for elections to 21 civic bodies, including the Agartala Municipal Corporation (AMC), ended.
The CPI(M) has fielded 263 candidates across 345 wards, while the Congress has nominated candidates in 221 wards after seat-sharing talks between the two INDIA bloc partners failed.

"The date for filing nominations for the civic elections ended yesterday, and scrutiny has begun. We are still hopeful of a seat adjustment with anti-BJP parties, as defeating the saffron party is our main political objective," Mr. Chaudhury told reporters.

Accusing the BJP of weakening democratic values in Tripura over the past nine years, the Leader of Opposition in the State Assembly said he had held discussions with the leadership of a major anti-BJP party on an electoral understanding.

"We emphasised seat adjustment with anti-BJP parties to avoid a split in the anti-BJP vote bank in the civic elections. A decision may be taken in the next two days, as the last date for withdrawal of nominations is November 10. The party is fully committed to preventing a split in anti-BJP votes in the State," he said.

Meanwhile, Left Front convener Manik Dey on Friday (November 6, 2026) alleged that party candidates were unable to file nominations in five civic bodies, Santirbazar, Ranirbazar, Jirania, Mohanpur and Kamalpur, due to alleged obstruction by ruling party leaders and supporters.
He also alleged that the police and the State Election Commission had failed to ensure security for Left Front candidates despite a Tripura High Court order.

Mr. Dey further claimed that five party supporters were injured in an attack by BJP supporters at Dukli in West Tripura district while campaigning for CPI(M) candidate Swapna Nath, who is contesting from AMC Ward 44.

articles.title: Wayanad landslides: Despite township progress, 13 Adivasi families still caught between ‘no-go zones’ and delayed rehab
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Some now live in rented accommodation with government assistance, cut off from their forest environment and traditional livelihoods. Others have returned to the forest, as construction of the promised houses on alternative land allocated to them at Puthiyavillage in Meppadi under Forest Rights Act, 2006 is yet to begin

Even as the rehabilitation of survivors of the 2024 Wayanad landslide (Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide) in Keralam is making progress, with 327 families, including 149 last month, having been allotted houses at the township project in Kalpetta, the resettlement and rebuilding of lives remain a distant prospect for 13 Adivasi families displaced in the aftermath of the disaster.

Though their homes were not damaged, the families had to leave as the areas surrounding their settlements fell within designated ‘no-go zones’ (unsuitable for habitation), with one of the settlements also falling in a ‘red zone’. Some now live in rented accommodation with government assistance, cut off from their forest environment and traditional livelihoods. Others have returned to the forest, as construction of the promised houses on alternative land allocated to them at Puthiyavillage in Meppadi under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 is yet to begin.

articles.title: Faith meets fitness: The Keralam church where prayers come with pull-ups
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, has set up an open gym to promote fitness among parishioners. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.

Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.

The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.

“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.

When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.

“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.

The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.

The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.

For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.

The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.

For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

articles.title: Congress Govt lifted more water from Godavari than the BRS government: Govt Whip Aadi Srinivas
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Harish Rao getting vicarious pleasure in drought conditions: Aadi Srinivas

Countering the BRS criticism that Godavari water was released to Andhra Pradesh, Government Whip Aadi Srinivas said the Congress government had lifted more water from the Godavari than the BRS government.

Presenting the figures at a press conference in Hyderabad on Saturday (November 7, 2026), he said the previous BRS government had lifted a total of 86.127 TMC of water through the Devadula project between 2014-15 and 2022-23, averaging 9.57 TMC annually.

In comparison, the Congress government had lifted around 68 TMC in the last three years, he claimed. It lifted 18.067 TMC in 2024-25 and 18.20 TMC in 2025-26, averaging 18.13 TMC annually, which was 89% higher than the average during the previous regime, he said. The government had already lifted 16.71 TMC during the first five months of the current year, he added.

Mr. Srinivas said 8.10 TMC had also been lifted through the Sitarama Sagar project, taking the total water lifted downstream of Kaleshwaram to 24.81 TMC. The water had been used to provide irrigation to lakhs of acres in Warangal, Nalgonda and Khammam districts, he claimed.

Explaining the Devadula project's capacity, he said it has 10 pumping units that could lift 0.23 TMC a day if operated continuously. He said it would take around four and a half days to lift one TMC of water, questioning Mr Harish Rao’s criticism of the quantum of water lifted.

He added that the government was temporarily blocking the flow of water near Dummugudem with sandbags and diverting it to meet drinking water needs. BRS leaders could visit the location and verify the arrangements, he added.

Referring to the condition of the Kaleshwaram project, Mr. Srinivas said the Medigadda barrage had suffered subsidence, while seepage problems had been reported at the Annaram and Sundilla barrages. In such circumstances, the BRS leader’s demand for lifting water at Medigadda was not practical, he said.

He claimed that the Ellampalli project, constructed during the Congress regime, was now proving beneficial to farmers. Had the previous BRS government constructed a barrage at Tummidihatti as originally planned, the present situation could have been avoided, he said.

He asked former Minister T. Harish Rao stop spreading misinformation about crop losses, power supply and irrigation, alleging that he was getting vicarious pleasure of the drought situation in the State.

On the Krishna River water dispute, Mr. Srinivas accused the previous BRS government of agreeing to an interim arrangement that allocated 512 TMC to Andhra Pradesh and 299 TMC to Telangana out of the 811 TMC share of undivided Andhra Pradesh. He said the Revanth Reddy government was now demanding a fair allocation of 558 TMC for Telangana.

articles.title: Who is Abdul El-Sayed, first Muslim U.S. Senator-elect?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Abdul El-Sayed is set to become the first Muslim to enter the U.S. Senate with his victory over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers in midterm elections

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat on Tuesday (November 4, 2026), according to media projections, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber and preserving a crucial Democratic seat in the party’s fight for Senate control.

His victory denied Republicans the chance to fill the seat left vacant by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. The 42-year-old former public health official ran on a progressive platform focused ⁠on lowering costs for working families and ⁠reducing corporate influence in politics.
His win marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing ‌in this closely contested midterm election cycle.

Abdul El-Sayed was born on October 31 , 1984, in Rochester Hills, Michigan, U.S.. He attended public schools, where he captained his high school football, wrestling and lacrosse teams. He was raised by his father, Mohamed, an Egyptian immigrant and his stepmom, Jackie, whose family has lived in Gratiot County, Michigan since the 1800s. Mr. El-Sayed earned his undergraduate degree with the highest distinction from the University of Michigan where he also played on the Wolverine men’s lacrosse team. He went on to earn a medical degree from Columbia University under an NIH-funded fellowship, as well as a second doctorate from Oxford University as Rhodes Scholer.
He lives in Ann Arbor with his wife, Dr. Sarah Jukaku and their two daughters.

Although trained as a physician, Mr. El-Sayed shifted his focus to public service after realising the political systemic issues that was deteriorating public health, according to his campaign website.

He rebuilt Detroit’s Health Department after bankruptcy and led Wayne County’s Department of Health. Human & Veterans Services, serving 1.8 million residents. His public service spans several achievements, including securing free eyeglasses for children, targeting major environmental polluters, making the life-saving Narcan universally accessible and pioneering a programme projected to cancel up to $700 million in medical debt for 3,00,000 Michiganders, as per the website.

He authored Medicare for All: A Citizen’s Guide and served on former President Biden’s 2020 Unity Task Force for Healthcare to help develop policies aimed at lowering prescription drug costs. His public service earned him recognition as “Public Official of the Year” by the Michigan LCV and also a spot on Crain’s Detroit Business 40 Under 40 list.

Mr. El-Sayed won the U.S. Senate seat in Michigan over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. He launched his campaign to lower living costs and ensure government agencies serve working people rather than billionaires.

Mr. Rogers, 63, ‌a former Congressman and FBI agent, entered ​the race with strong backing from President Trump and national Republicans and sought ⁠to cast Mr. El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to Islamic extremism through alleged ties to the Muslim ‌Brotherhood, claims that Mr. El-Sayed denies and that remain unsupported by evidence. Democrats said the attacks on Mr. El-Sayed relied on Islamophobic tropes, according to Reuters.

Mr. Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with Mr. El-Sayed’s opposition to U.S. military ‌aid for Israel and his characterisation of Israel’s actions in ​Gaza as genocide.

But Mr. Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and ⁠President Trump’s low ratings. In the closing weeks of ⁠the race, he broke with the President on the war in Iran and the ‌U.S. trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs ​for businesses and consumers.

articles.title: U.S. midterm election results: Senate, House and Governor shifts before and after
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Democrats surged to full control of Congress in the November 2026 U.S. midterm elections, flipping the Senate and House after winning net seats across key battlegrounds and sweeping into Republican strongholds. Here’s what changed between 2022 and 2026 midterms.

The November U.S. midterm elections saw a major shift in Washington’s power dynamic as Democrats captured full control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, by crossing the 218-seat threshold needed for a majority.

In contrast to the 2022 midterms, where former President Joe Biden’s Democrats defied expected losses by holding the Senate and narrowly losing the House, the 2026 midterms saw Democrats gain full control of both chambers of Congress.

The almost dramatic swing towards Democrats, by the very same voters in the conservative bastion that propelled President Donald Trump to a second term just two years ago, is a result of widespread discontent over economic pressures including high living costs along with foreign policy decisions regarding the war with Iran. Voters elected Democratic candidates across the conservative strongholds and swing states creating a divided government under Mr. Trump.

In the 2022 midterms, pre-election predictions pointed toward a powerful “red wave” favouring Republicans due to surging inflation and low approval ratings for Mr. Biden. But the wave failed to fully materialise. Democrats defied the trends by retaining control of the Senate (reaching 50 seats after picking up Pennsylvania and holding Nevada), though Republicans narrowly flipped control of the House of Representatives with a slim majority.
In the 2026 midterms, the story was different. Democrats scored a sweeping victory over the ruling party, seizing control of both Senate and the House of Representatives.
In 2022 midterm elections, Democrats entered the election with a 50-50 split (with Vice-President Kamala Harris as the tiebreaker) and expanded their narrow control.

They gained a net seat by flipping Pennsylvania (where Democrat John Fetterman defeated Mehmet Oz) and secured a majority by holding Nevada (Catherine Cortez Masto), finishing with 50 seats to Republicans’ 49.

In 2026, Democrats captured full control of the 100-seat upper chamber by making historic inroads into Republican strongholds. The Democratic Caucus has currently secured 54 seats to achieve majority after defending its existing seats and winning key races, while the Republican Caucus has secured 44 seats. The counting is still under way.

Major wins include James Talarico gaining a Senate seat in Texas, Kansas electing its first Democratic Senator since the Great Depression and Democrats defeating Mr. Trump’s handpicked candidate in South Carolina (Democrat Annie Andrews ousting Republican Darline Graham).

In 2022, Republicans gained control of the House, gaining nine net seats to secure a narrow majority of 222 seats compared to the Democrats’ 213 seats, crossing the majority mark of 218 seats in the 435-seat chamber. This narrow margin of victory was potentially close to the 221–212 margin seen in 2001.

Meanwhile, in 2026, Democrats reversed those gains in a nationwide rout. Democrats have officially won 239 seats, surpassing the 218 needed for a majority. Republicans have secured 147 seats. The final counts are still being finalised.

Gubernatorial contests saw Democrats pick up two net Governor’s mansions in 2022, maintaining 24 governorships to the Republicans’ 26. Before the election, Republicans held a 28 to 22 seat advantage. Also, voters in 2022 rejected election-denier candidates in battleground State races for Governor, Secretary of State and Attorney General (with 12 out of 13 such candidates losing).

articles.title: How improving your daily lifestyle can help decrease the risk of endometrial cancer

fullParagraphs: The incidence of endometrial cancer is rising in India. Understanding risk factors can help women take action to reduce their risk, and make informed decisions about their health

When people think of cancer, factors such as genetics and family history often come to mind. However, for endometrial cancer, everyday lifestyle choices can also play a significant role. Understanding these risk factors can help women make informed decisions about their health.

Endometrial cancer, which begins in the endometrium, that is, the inner lining of the uterus, is one of the most common gynaecological cancers in developed countries. Over the past several years, its incidence has been rising in India. It is mostly diagnosed after menopause, but other conditions can also increase risk.

fullParagraphs: The U.S. regulators warned organisations about “ongoing cyber threat activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems,” shortly after these hacks led to huge amounts of food waste across European supermarkets
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and government regulators on Thursday (November 5, 2026) issued a warning about cyber-attacks targeting industrial coolers and fridges.
The warning acknowledged that hackers were targeting vulnerabilities in unpatched or internet-linked refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.
Gaining control of these systems would enable hackers to adjust temperatures to dangerous extremes or run unauthorised defrost cycles, leading to the spoilage of inventory or even fire hazards.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DOT) warned organisations about “ongoing cyber threat activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems.”

The U.S. FBI-issued factsheet recommended that organisations with cold storage facilities de-link control system devices from the internet, enhance password security, apply patches to keep systems updated, and replace legacy devices that no longer receive security updates.

The notice came shortly after cyber attacks led to huge amounts of food waste across European supermarket franchises, where some fridge temperatures were raised as high as 50 degrees Celsius in October.
Food and produce had to be thrown out at a mass scale, along with large quantities of melted ice.
The perpetrators behind the attacks have not yet been identified or apprehended.

“Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors. We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman.

articles.title: A sub-adult elephant found dead in Shankara Range in Shivamogga
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Officials suspect the animal was electrocuted after coming into contact with a live electric wire along the edge of a paddy field
A sub-adult male elephant, aged about 10 to 12 years, was found dead at Ichavadi village in the Shankara Range of Shivamogga Division on Saturday (November 7, 2026).
Officials suspect the animal was electrocuted after coming into contact with a live electric wire along the edge of a paddy field.

Officers from the Shankara Range and Shivamogga Division visited the spot. During the preliminary inquiry, they questioned Alimiya, a resident of the village, according to a press communique issued by the Deputy Conservator of Forests, Shivamogga Division.

The suspect told the officers that he had erected a fence and connected it to a power supply to protect his ripening paddy crop from wild boar. A case has been registered under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.

The Forest Department has also asked MESCOM officials to initiate action against the accused under the Electricity Act. The statement added that the carcass will be disposed of in accordance with the standard operating procedure.

articles.title: Sonia Gandhi interview: ‘Great damage done to the fabric of India by BJP’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Ahead of the launch of her book, Sonia Gandhi speaks to The Hindu, answering a number of questions — personal and political

In this wide-ranging interview to The Hindu on her soon-to-be-launched book, Belonging: A Journey of Love , published by HarperCollins India, Sonia Gandhi responds in writing to a number of questions, personal, historical, and political, raised by N. Ram.

The subjects covered include how she came to write her story about belonging; the values she grew up with and came to learn and cherish in India; what she learnt from Rajiv Gandhi and Indira Gandhi and how they shaped her life and outlook; the “great damage … done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions” by the BJP-RSS dispensation; how she viewed, and now looks back on, the Emergency of 1975-1977; the major political decisions she made to accept the office of Congress President in 1998 and to continue in it, after a challenge by some colleagues, in 1999, and in 2004 to decline the offer to become Prime Minister; the current political situation and the prospects of the Congress and its coalition partners; and the change of publisher in India just weeks before the book’s launch.

‘Others have spent decades telling my “story”,’ you posted on X the other day, ‘now it’s my turn.’ My AI-assisted bibliographical search suggests there are at least 75 books, including several biographies, that attempt or purport to tell your story in substantial measure. Your post hints that you were amused rather than irritated or angry about others presuming to tell your story. Am I right? And did you read those books, or at least some of them, written by biographers and others who spent decades telling your ‘story’?

I had no idea there were so many! But I have never felt like reading books about myself. A long time ago Rajiv and I realised that there was no point in trying to keep up with all that had been written about us. But, as I say in the book, there came a time when I felt that I should tell my own story.

In the Prologue to Belonging , you give us an insight into how you came to write your story, ‘perhaps…a story worth sharing,’ as you put it somewhat self-deprecatingly. Was it the ‘chorus’, which was on your case for years, or something within you, or both that eventually pushed you over the line to give us this intimate and unusually candid story? And may I ask how long it took you to write the book, breaks and all?

It’s been such a long time that I’ve lost track, but it has certainly been more than a decade since I first wrote a bit. I only started writing in earnest about five years ago. It wasn’t an uninterrupted process. There were times when words and thoughts flowed, others when nothing would come out, and I would throw my hands up in frustration.

You describe Belonging as a personal memoir, with politics providing the background or ‘a kind of framework’. But it’s really a love story at its heart and that’s how I read it. The story of an extraordinary, instantly formed magnetic bond of love between Rajiv and Sonia, which gradually grew into something much larger, drawing you into the highest circles of power, then reluctantly into public life and politics, and eventually making you one of the country’s foremost political leaders. Stranger than fiction, isn’t it?

Yes! That’s one reason I had no desire to talk about it for so long. But it is not only a love story between the two of us, it’s also the story of how I grew to love Rajiv’s family and the country to which they belonged, and then I too came to belong in it. And of how this love brought me into public life, when I saw the purpose of all the sacrifices they had made being threatened, and the party was weakening. I felt I had to do something.

The writer R.K. Narayan once observed that, despite the passage of time and physical ageing, ‘the chap inside is the same,’ capturing the enduring sense of self. You grew up in a small town in Italy, in a family and social environment far removed from the world that you would eventually inhabit and make your own. Looking back over more than six decades in India, how much of that young Italian woman survives in the person you are today?

The values that I learnt growing up survive. I have tried my best to be true to them: loyalty to family and friends, sincerity and feeling for others, the idea of being dutiful and responsible. I think I can say that in these I am the same person Rajiv met sixty years ago. But I used to smile and laugh a lot more then!

Rajiv Gandhi, the love of your life, and Indira Gandhi, with whom you shared an exceptionally close bond, are central figures in your story. Looking back, what do you see as their defining qualities and the ways in which each shaped your life and outlook?

When I arrived in India as a young bride, I knew nothing about India. All that I am and know today, I learnt from them. Their courage, their empathy, their commitment to a secular and democratic India and most of all, the pull of duty that was greater than any other for both of them was something that inspired me and held me steadfast during times of difficulty and doubt.

articles.title: Voter ID for welfare? What Rajiv Ranjan Singh’s proposal could mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Opposition parties have linked this announcement to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, in which 13.5 crore electors were reportedly removed. They argue that disenfranchisement will now be coupled with exclusion from welfare programmes.

Story so far: Union Minister for Panchayati Raj and senior JD(U) leader Rajiv Ranjan Singh, alias Lalan Singh, on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) said that voter cards, along with biometric authentication, will be the basis for identifying beneficiaries and processing payments for welfare schemes. He argued that Aadhaar cards can be easily made at every street corner, implying that they can lead to fraudulent beneficiaries. He presented the use of voter cards along with biometric authentication as a possible mechanism to deal with such cases.

The ration card was the first mass-scale identity document, introduced during colonial rule just a few years before the eclipse of the Empire. Welfare entitlements came to be linked to stable residences and enumerated households. It was the first time that both a residential address and a household were formally enumerated, giving a singular identity to the Indian family.

articles.title: Congress pushing Telangana towards ‘Asset bankruptcy’, alleges BJP leader Gudur
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Congress government is pushing Telangana towards “asset bankruptcy” by relying on auctions of valuable government lands to meet its immediate revenue requirements, alleged senior BJP leader Gudur Narayana Reddy.

In a statement made at Hyderabad, he warned that continued disposal of public assets could weaken the State’s financial credibility, constrain its future borrowing capacity and affect its ability to finance welfare schemes and infrastructure projects.

Citing CAG-related figures, Mr. Narayana Reddy said Telangana received ₹16,478 crore from land, property, and miscellaneous sources in 2023-24, accounting for about 69% of its non-tax revenue. He said the erstwhile TSIIC had 53,473.76 acres as of March 31, 2022, and had made 2,355 land allotments covering around 4,050 acres between 2014-15 and 2021-22.

He pointed out that the BRS government had auctioned about 31 acres in the Raidurg-Knowledge City corridor for nearly ₹730 crore, while land prices at Kokapet Neopolis had touched ₹100.75 crore per acre in August 2023.

The BJP leader alleged that the Congress government had intensified the process since coming to power. He claimed that since January 2024, the Congress government had auctioned nearly 40 acres in Raidurg-Knowledge City for about ₹7,000 crore, at an average of ₹179 crore per acre. He also cited auction prices of ₹177 crore per acre in October 2025, ₹237 crore in May 2026 and ₹264 crore and ₹269 crore in August 2026.
Similarly, the three-phase HMDA auctions at Kokapet Neopolis in 2025 had fetched around ₹3,708 crore for 27 acres, averaging ₹137 crore per acre, he said.

Referring to HMDA’s proposal to auction another 114 land parcels with an estimated revenue target of ₹2,000 crore, he questioned the rationale behind continuing to depend on land sales for revenue mobilisation.
He also expressed concern about the implications for future industrial development, noting that, as of September 2025, TGIIC reportedly had 5,730 acres available for industrial allotment.

🏛️ National & Polity 📅 07 Nov 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

Congress pushing Telangana towards ‘Asset bankruptcy’, alleges BJP leader Gudur

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

Congress government is pushing Telangana towards “asset bankruptcy” by relying on auctions of valuable government lands to meet its immediate revenue requirements, alleged senior BJP leader Gudur Narayana Reddy.

In a statement made at Hyderabad, he warned that continued disposal of public assets could weaken the State’s financial credibility, constrain its future borrowing capacity and affect its ability to finance welfare schemes and infrastructure projects.

Citing CAG-related figures, Mr. Narayana Reddy said Telangana received ₹16,478 crore from land, property, and miscellaneous sources in 2023-24, accounting for about 69% of its non-tax revenue. He said the erstwhile TSIIC had 53,473.76 acres as of March 31, 2022, and had made 2,355 land allotments covering around 4,050 acres between 2014-15 and 2021-22.

He pointed out that the BRS government had auctioned about 31 acres in the Raidurg-Knowledge City corridor for nearly ₹730 crore, while land prices at Kokapet Neopolis had touched ₹100.75 crore per acre in August 2023.

The BJP leader alleged that the Congress government had intensified the process since coming to power. He claimed that since January 2024, the Congress government had auctioned nearly 40 acres in Raidurg-Knowledge City for about ₹7,000 crore, at an average of ₹179 crore per acre. He also cited auction prices of ₹177 crore per acre in October 2025, ₹237 crore in May 2026 and ₹264 crore and ₹269 crore in August 2026.

Similarly, the three-phase HMDA auctions at Kokapet Neopolis in 2025 had fetched around ₹3,708 crore for 27 acres, averaging ₹137 crore per acre, he said.

Referring to HMDA’s proposal to auction another 114 land parcels with an estimated revenue target of ₹2,000 crore, he questioned the rationale behind continuing to depend on land sales for revenue mobilisation.

He also expressed concern about the implications for future industrial development, noting that, as of September 2025, TGIIC reportedly had 5,730 acres available for industrial allotment.

articles.title: Siang dam protesters released in Arunachal Pradesh after nearly month in detention
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The four, identified as Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, were detained on October 9 under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014

Four protesters detained over the proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh were released from Jully Central Jail near Itanagar on Saturday (November 7, 2026), nearly a month after their arrest, officials said.
The four, identified as Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, were detained on October 9 under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014, they added.

Their release came a day after the State Government agreed to free them as a goodwill gesture while responding to demands raised by the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum (SIFF), which has been leading the protest against the proposed mega dam.
The development marks a significant step towards easing tensions in the Siang Valley, where opposition to the project has triggered protests and confrontations in recent months.

In a letter dated November 6, the Chief Minister's Office (CMO) also approved the reinstatement of suspended gaonburas and gaonburis affected by disciplinary action in connection with the SUMP agitation.
The Government, however, maintained that the withdrawal of FIRs against protesters would have to follow due legal process.

It also said the demand for withdrawal of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) and Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel from the region would be discussed during the proposed meeting with SIFF representatives, taking into account the prevailing security situation.
The Government has urged SIFF to resume dialogue and communicate a convenient date, along with a list of delegates, for a proposed meeting with Chief Minister Pema Khandu.
It also appealed to the organisation to encourage residents of Siang and Upper Siang districts to maintain peace and refrain from violence, intimidation and attacks.

The CMO's communication, signed by Shibu Thomas, Principal Private Secretary to the Chief Minister, reiterated the government's commitment to addressing the concerns of the Adi community through a mutually acceptable roadmap.
The release of the four protesters was among SIFF's key demands before agreeing to participate in talks with the government.
The forum had earlier rejected Mr. Khandu's invitation for dialogue, insisting that its demands, including the release of detainees and withdrawal of security forces, be addressed first.

articles.title: Under-construction roof of school auditorium collapses in Keralam; no casualties
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The incident occurred around noon at PKS Higher Secondary School, Kanjiramkulam, near Neyyattinkara. The roofing work was carried out on Friday, but heavy rain later affected the structure, officials said
An under-construction roof of an auditorium at an aided school in Keralam collapsed on Saturday (November 7, 2026). However, no one was injured, officials said.
The incident occurred around noon at PKS Higher Secondary School, Kanjiramkulam, near Neyyattinkara, Education department officials said.
The auditorium had a tin-sheet roof, and work was underway to replace it with a concrete structure.
The roofing work was carried out on Friday, but heavy rain later affected the structure, officials said.
The entire concrete roof structure, including the steel bars and supporting poles, collapsed, they said.
As it was not a working day, there were no students on the premises.
The workers present at the site managed to move to safety after noticing the roof collapsing, officials said.
Work has begun to clear the debris, and Public Works Department officials will examine whether any defects in the construction work led to the collapse, officials added.

articles.title: Vance distancing himself from Trump ahead of 2028 Presidential race: Ex-U.S. NSA Bolton
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Bolton described Vance's remarks as "very wrong" and a "big political mistake", saying the Republicans overlooked broader voter dissatisfaction with the economy, rising prices, and Trump's tariff policies

U.S. Vice President J. D. Vance is trying to distance himself from President Donald Trump by blaming the Republicans' midterm losses on the Iran war as he prepares for a potential 2028 Presidential bid, former U.S. national security adviser John Bolton has said.

In an interview with PTI Videos , Mr. Bolton described Mr. Vance's remarks as "very wrong" and a "big political mistake", saying the Republicans overlooked broader voter dissatisfaction with the economy, rising prices, and Mr. Trump's tariff policies.

"There's no doubt that part of the underlying reason for Mr. Vance’s statement was that this is the beginning of his 2028 nomination campaign. And he's trying something very politically risky here," he said.
Mr. Bolton argued that the Iran war was only one factor behind voter discontent, pointing out that Mr. Trump's tariffs had contributed to persistently high prices.
He said Mr. Trump had promised during the 2024 Presidential campaign to address economic concerns better than the Biden administration, but had failed to deliver after taking office.

"The voters took him at his word. They said we have more faith that Mr. Trump can handle these issues than Mr. Biden and Ms. Harris. So he gets elected, he comes in, and he doesn't do it. And if anything, he's causing more problems," the former U.S. NSA said.

Mr. Bolton also emphasised how the Iran war pushed up international oil and gas prices and increased energy costs for American consumers. "What they opposed was the higher price of gasoline. And Mr. Trump didn't even attempt to address that," he added.

He described the Democrats' strong midterm performance as a "stinging repudiation" of Mr. Trump, saying voters across party lines were tired of his leadership, though the results did not necessarily amount to an endorsement of the blue team.
He also said Mr. Trump was unlikely to fundamentally change his leadership style during the remaining two years of his term, despite the electoral setback.
"Trump's whole operating style for 10 years is: I don't work with anybody. I represent the people, and I'm going to do what I want to do," Mr. Bolton stated.
He further warned that a Democratic-controlled Congress could launch investigations into the Trump administration, including allegations of corruption, self-dealing and self-enrichment.

On U.S.-India ties, Mr. Bolton said domestic political turmoil in Washington could push foreign policy priorities to the sidelines, affecting discussions on defence cooperation and common security challenges in the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new Chief of Staff?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Stephen Miller, one of U.S. President Donald Trump’s closest aides for decades, will replace Susie Wiles, who becomes the first major White House casualty from the Democratic landslide earlier this week

U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday (November 6, 2026) named Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new Chief of Staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback after Republicans were hammered in the midterms.

Ultra-loyalist Miller, 41, will replace Susie Wiles, who becomes the first major White House casualty from the Democratic landslide earlier this week . In a post on Truth Social announcing Mr. Miller’s appointment, Mr. Trump described him as “one of my most trusted advisors”.

Stephen Miller, a key member of Mr. Trump’s inner circle, is a prominent architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies. Known for his sharp suits and sunglasses, Miller has been one of Mr. Trump’s closest aides for decades and longest-serving advisers, pushing nativist policies that gelled with the President’s “America First” agenda.

Mr. Miller currently serves as White House Deputy Chief of Staff and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, he is most closely aligned with the President’s immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration. He is also a former aide to hardliner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who would go on to serve as Mr. Trump’s first Attorney General.

Mr. Miller was raised in politically liberal Santa Monica, California, but developed a reputation as a combative conservative as a columnist at Duke University’s student newspaper. ⁠As a congressional aide in the 2010s, he was an early advocate for restricting immigration at a time when that was not a mainstream position in the Republican Party.

He joined Mr. Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, then served ‌as an advisor and speechwriter in his first 2017-2021 term. After Mr. Trump lost the 2020 election, Mr. Miller founded the conservative advocacy group America First Legal, filing complaints that accused companies ‌such as Nike of discriminating against white people.
His wife, Katie Miller, is a conservative podcaster and former ⁠communications aide in Mr. Trump’s first administration.
As Mr. Trump’s Deputy Chief of Staff for policy and homeland security advisor, he was the brains behind the mass deportation programme that defined the first year of the President’s second term.

Mr. Miller is best known for driving the immigration crackdown, setting a target of 3,000 arrests per day — far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to target anybody in the country illegally, ‌not just those with criminal records.
But he faced widespread criticism after the deadly shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January — incidents that sparked mass demonstrations.

Beyond enforcement, Mr. Miller has been a vocal advocate for ending birthright citizenship, and denounced the ⁠Supreme Court’s ruling that rejected that proposal as “one of the most destructive and outrageous decisions” in the court’s history.
Mr. Miller announced a ban on “birth tourism” after that ruling, seeking to prevent people from coming to the ‌United States to deliver babies.

🌐 International Affairs 📅 07 Nov 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new Chief of Staff?

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics

Stephen Miller, one of U.S. President Donald Trump’s closest aides for decades, will replace Susie Wiles, who becomes the first major White House casualty from the Democratic landslide earlier this week

U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday (November 6, 2026) named Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new Chief of Staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback after Republicans were hammered in the midterms.

Ultra-loyalist Miller, 41, will replace Susie Wiles, who becomes the first major White House casualty from the Democratic landslide earlier this week . In a post on Truth Social announcing Mr. Miller’s appointment, Mr. Trump described him as “one of my most trusted advisors”.

Stephen Miller, a key member of Mr. Trump’s inner circle, is a prominent architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies. Known for his sharp suits and sunglasses, Miller has been one of Mr. Trump’s closest aides for decades and longest-serving advisers, pushing nativist policies that gelled with the President’s “America First” agenda.

Mr. Miller currently serves as White House Deputy Chief of Staff and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, he is most closely aligned with the President’s immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration. He is also a former aide to hardliner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who would go on to serve as Mr. Trump’s first Attorney General.

Mr. Miller was raised in politically liberal Santa Monica, California, but developed a reputation as a combative conservative as a columnist at Duke University’s student newspaper. ⁠As a congressional aide in the 2010s, he was an early advocate for restricting immigration at a time when that was not a mainstream position in the Republican Party.

He joined Mr. Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, then served ‌as an advisor and speechwriter in his first 2017-2021 term. After Mr. Trump lost the 2020 election, Mr. Miller founded the conservative advocacy group America First Legal, filing complaints that accused companies ‌such as Nike of discriminating against white people.

His wife, Katie Miller, is a conservative podcaster and former ⁠communications aide in Mr. Trump’s first administration.

As Mr. Trump’s Deputy Chief of Staff for policy and homeland security advisor, he was the brains behind the mass deportation programme that defined the first year of the President’s second term.

Mr. Miller is best known for driving the immigration crackdown, setting a target of 3,000 arrests per day — far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to target anybody in the country illegally, ‌not just those with criminal records.

But he faced widespread criticism after the deadly shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January — incidents that sparked mass demonstrations.

Beyond enforcement, Mr. Miller has been a vocal advocate for ending birthright citizenship, and denounced the ⁠Supreme Court’s ruling that rejected that proposal as “one of the most destructive and outrageous decisions” in the court’s history.

Mr. Miller announced a ban on “birth tourism” after that ruling, seeking to prevent people from coming to the ‌United States to deliver babies.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday (November 6, 2026) named Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new Chief of Staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback after Republicans were hammered in the midterms.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Mr. Miller announced a ban on “birth tourism” after that ruling, seeking to prevent people from coming to the ‌United States to deliver babies.

On Wednesday (November 4, 2026), rising tensions in Asuncion, the capital of Paraguay, turned violent as hundreds of thousands stormed the streets to protest locking out of their accounts in the country’s biggest bank. As fires burned and people anxiously queued outside the collapsed bank, President Santiago Pena, a former shareholder in the bank, announced his resignation.

But as Congress moved to impeach him, Mr. Pena disappeared amid rumours that he had fled to Argentina — just as Brazilian far-right leader Flávio Bolsonaro did last week before fleeing to U.S. after losing the election to President Lula da Silva. “We have information that he left the country without telling anyone. I think he went to Argentina and sought asylum,” said Paraguayan Senator Antonio Velázquez on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

articles.title: The science behind sleep supplements - melatonin and magnesium
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Doctors warn that there is no replacement for natural solutions, and supplements cannot be taken over a long period

If a good night’s sleep has become your holy grail, who are the knights in shining armour you will employ to reach that chalice? Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?

The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

articles.title: At COP31, the ‘overshoot’ narrative cannot replace climate action
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: No COP decision has referred to the quantitative value of the total or remaining carbon budget nor has discussed which countries have spent it the most. If COP31 is to deliver real impetus to climate action, its decisions must revert to the basics

COP31 is around the corner, marking the end of a year of extreme weather events, terrible human tragedy, as well as a severe energy crisis. It is also the year in which the world is preparing to officially accept that we will exceed a warming level of 1.5 degrees celsius.

The natural corollary to this unassailable reality is that countries should strive to collectively limit warming to as little over 1.5 degrees celsius, and as below 2 degrees, as possible. This requires scientific discussions, assessment of options, and a critical analysis of the trade-offs. However, what we have instead is another buzz word: ‘overshoot’.
